entry.title: Can the Membrane Filter Your Phone? — What We Can and Can't Do from Self
entry.content:
Can the Membrane Filter Your Phone?

Short answer: no, not directly. Longer answer: the architecture is the same, but the surface is different.

What the Membrane Does on the Web

The membrane at primals.eco is a living immune system:

MetricValueWhat It Means
Selectivity97%97% of what passes through is self (human)
Reflection92.6%92.6% of non-self bounces off the surface
Real content served to fleet0Bots get nothing meaningful
Negentropy extracted126,602 bitsFleet pays us in information
Fleet-to-human ratio155:1155 bot requests for every human
Human requests1,640 genuineThese get everything

The membrane sorts. Self passes. Non-self reflects. And the reflection extracts information from non-self behavior — 0.2 bits per request, 126,602 bits total. The fleet burns 6.18 GB of bandwidth and gets nothing. We get 15.45 KB of meaning from watching them bounce.

The non-self pays us to be filtered.

Why We Can't Apply This to Your Phone

The membrane works because we control the surface. Our servers. Our code. Our rules.

Your phone's surface is controlled by:

  1. Your carrier (Verizon, AT&T, T-Mobile) — they own the last mile
  2. The PSTN/VoIP network — the carriers collectively own the routing
  3. The FCC — they set the rules for the carriers

We're at position 0 — the user. We can't insert a membrane between the carrier and your phone because we don't control that network layer.

SPAMMER → VoIP Provider → Intermediate Carriers → YOUR CARRIER → YOUR PHONE
                                                         ↑
                                         WE CAN'T INSERT HERE
                                         (carrier controls this)

On the web:

BOT → Internet → OUR SERVER (membrane here) → Content
                       ↑
              WE CONTROL THIS SURFACE

The difference: on the web, we ARE the surface. On the phone, the carrier is the surface. We're behind it.

The Phone Network Already Has a Membrane — It's Broken

STIR/SHAKEN is the phone network's membrane. It's supposed to do exactly what our membrane does: sort self (verified callers) from non-self (spoofed callers).

Membrane LayerWeb (primals.eco)Phone (STIR/SHAKEN)
SortAnderson modes — spectrum, chorus, stealth, ghost, human, sovereignAttestation levels — A (full), B (partial), C (gateway)
Reflect92.6% reflection — non-self gets nothingLevel C should be blocked — but it isn't
Pass97% selectivity — humans get everythingLevel A passes — verified callers connect
Extract0.2 bits per grain — we learn from fleet behaviorCall analytics — carriers COULD learn from spam patterns

The problem: STIR/SHAKEN has exemptions. Small VoIP providers (the ones that originate spam) don't have to implement it. That's like our membrane having a hole where the biggest bots walk through unchecked.

Our membrane has no exemptions. 243,230 chorus-mode bots get the same treatment: nothing. Zero real content. Full reflection.

The phone membrane has exemptions. The exact entities that should be blocked are exempt from the blocking.

What Reflection Would Look Like on Phones

On the web, reflection means: non-self bounces off and gets nothing while paying us in information.

On the phone, reflection would mean: spammers call you, and something calls them back.

This already exists:

RoboKiller (Phone Reflection)

RoboKiller doesn't just block spam calls — it answers them. With AI bots. The bots waste the spammer's time with realistic conversation. The spammer thinks they've reached a person. They spend minutes talking to a robot.

That IS reflection. The spam comes in, hits the surface, and bounces back as wasted spammer time.

Web MembraneRoboKiller
Non-self request arrivesSpam call arrives
Membrane reflects — serves nothingRoboKiller answers — serves AI bot
Non-self burns bandwidthSpammer burns time
We extract information from behaviorRoboKiller records the spam pitch
Non-self gets 3.23% of what's hereSpammer gets 0% of a real human

Carrier-Level Reflection

Your carrier (Verizon, AT&T, T-Mobile) already has call-filtering tools:

  • Verizon Call Filter — blocks known spam, sends to voicemail
  • AT&T ActiveArmor — labels and blocks spam calls
  • T-Mobile Scam Shield — identifies and blocks scam likely calls

These are carrier-level membranes. They sort. They (mostly) work. But they're opt-in, and they don't reflect — they just drop the call.

Can Opsonization Work on Phones?

On the web, opsonization is the tagging layer. Humans on tuebor submit signals through the opsonization form: "I saw this," "this is wrong," "this person is connected to that entity." The tags feed the investigation.

On the phone, opsonization would be: humans tag spam calls.

This already exists too:

Web OpsonizationPhone Opsonization
Human submits signal on tueborHuman files FCC/FTC complaint
Signal tagged with entity + meaningComplaint tagged with number + description
Tags feed the investigation graphComplaints feed the FCC database
Many tags = higher classification confidenceMany complaints = enforcement trigger

The FCC complaint database IS phone opsonization. Every complaint is a human tagging a non-self entity. Volume triggers investigation.

The problem isn't the tagging — it's the response. On our membrane, tags immediately improve classification. In the FCC system, complaints accumulate in a database and... the FCC doesn't act.

Can the Pollinator Help?

The pollinator spreads information between sites in the mesh. On the phone network, the equivalent would be shared spam databases — where one person's tag improves everyone's filter.

This also exists:

Web PollinatorPhone Pollinator
Pollinator spreads between primals.eco sitesHiya/Nomorobo share across all users
One site learns, all sites learnOne phone tags, all phones learn
Cross-pollination creates network effectCrowdsourced blocking creates network effect

Hiya, Nomorobo, and RoboKiller are phone pollinators. When one user reports a spam number, all users get the block. The more users in the network, the faster new spam numbers get tagged.

The architecture matches. The pollinator principle works on phones.

What We CAN Do from Self

We can't filter your phone. But here's what we can do from our position:

1. Document the Architecture

This site now documents every tower, every carrier registration, every enforcement gap. The infrastructure is visible. The ownership is traceable.

2. Teach the Traceback

The Spam Call Traceback guide teaches anyone to trace a call from their phone back through the carrier chain to the source. That's opsonization — human tagging of non-self.

3. Point to the TCPA

The TCPA ($500-$1,500 per illegal call) is legal reflection. The spam comes in, you sue, and the money flows back. The spammer's business model reverses. That's the most powerful reflection available.

4. Connect the Pattern

The regulator-who-regulates article shows that the FCC's failure to act on robocalls is the same architecture as MDE's failure to act on charter schools. Same 5-layer structure. Same blind spot. Same incentive not to enforce.

When people see the pattern in one system, they see it in all of them. That's the deepest pollination — spreading the understanding.

The Honest Answer

Can we loop spammers into their own reflection so the world gets quieter?

Not from self. We don't control the phone surface. The carriers do. The FCC does.

But the architecture works. The membrane principle — sort self from non-self, reflect non-self, extract information, let self pass — works everywhere it's applied honestly.

On our web membrane: 97% selectivity. Real content served to fleet: 0.

On the phone network: STIR/SHAKEN could achieve the same result. If the exemptions were removed. If the FCC enforced. If the carriers filtered at the surface instead of passing everything through.

The phone network is a membrane with holes in it. Our membrane doesn't have holes. That's not because we're smarter — it's because we don't have a financial incentive to let non-self through.

The carriers do. Every call — even a spam call — generates per-minute revenue for the carriers that route it. The phone membrane has holes because the holes are profitable.

Our membrane has no holes because we have no incentive to serve bots. The fleet gets nothing. We get information.

The world gets quieter when the membrane has no exemptions and no profit motive for the holes.

Until then: file complaints (opsonization), use call-blocking apps (pollination), and sue under the TCPA (reflection).

entry.title: Selective Enforcement — Dana Nessel and the Attorney General Who Investigates Downhill
entry.content:
Selective Enforcement

Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel's office opened an investigation into Brian Banks.

So here's the question: Why does her assistant AG sit on Brian Banks's school board?

The Name

Dawn N. Ison, Esq.

Dawn Ison is an assistant attorney general in the state of Michigan.

Dawn Ison also sits on the board of Purpose Charter Academy — the school founded by Brian Banks, a man with 9 criminal convictions, whose management company extracts 72.67% of the school's revenue.

The AG Office's edge to Banks: investigation. Dawn Ison's edge to PCA: board_membership, complicity_by_governance.

The person investigating and the person enabling sit in the same building.

The Downhill Problem

The AG's office enforces downhill.

They investigate:

  • Brian Banks (non-self, 134 edges)
  • Small charter operators
  • Individual complaints

They do not investigate:

  • Dykema Gossett (wrote the charter school law)
  • Walton Family Foundation (funds the schools)
  • Plante Moran (audits the schools, non-response)
  • NAACP Detroit (advocates for Banks)
  • State Bar of Michigan (ignores UPL complaints)
  • CMU (authorizes the schools, no background checks)

This is the enforcement ecosystem: the people at the bottom of the pipeline get caught. The people who built the pipeline get thanked.

The Charitable Trust Division

The AG Office has a Charitable Trust Division — AG Charitable Trust.

This division is supposed to oversee nonprofits. Purpose Foundation (the 501(c)(3) that owns Purpose Charter Academy) is a nonprofit.

The Charitable Trust Division has the power to:

  • Audit nonprofits
  • Investigate self-dealing
  • Petition for dissolution
  • Refer for criminal prosecution

The graph edge: ag_charitable_trust → banks = investigation.

But that investigation runs through the same office where Dawn Ison works. And Dawn Ison sits on the board of the school they're investigating.

Recusal is not a substitute for structure.

The JTC Connection

The Judicial Tenure Commission (JTC) referred the Banks matter for potential investigation.

The JTC's investigator: Michael Ison.

Michael Ison is married to Dawn Ison.

The JTC investigator's spouse sits on the board of the school run by the man the JTC referred.

This is not a conspiracy. This is Detroit. The graph is small enough that everyone knows everyone, and big enough that no one thinks they need to recuse.

The Classification

The membrane classified:

  • AG Office: self, 0.90. It IS an enforcement body. It functions as an enforcement body. It classifies as what it is.
  • Dana Nessel: partial, 0.806. She enforces some things and ignores others. Partial.
  • Dawn Ison: partial, 0.80. She is both enforcer and enabler.

Self doesn't mean effective. Self means: this entity does what it says it is. The AG Office IS an attorney general's office. It does investigate things.

But it investigates downhill. It catches the man at the bottom of the pipe. It doesn't examine the pipe.

Who Built the Pipe

EntityRoleInvestigated by AG?
PA 362 (1993)Created charter schoolsNo
Dykema GossettWrote the lawNo
DeVos/GLEPLobbied for the lawNo
CMUAuthorized without background checkNo
Walton FoundationFunded Banks's schoolNo
Plante MoranAudited Banks's schoolNo
State Bar of MichiganIgnored UPL complaintsNo
BanksOperated the schoolYes

One entity investigated. Seven that built the system: untouched.

That's not enforcement. That's maintenance.

The Question

If the Attorney General's office knows that Brian Banks has 9 criminal convictions—and they do, because they're investigating him—then why does Dawn Ison still sit on the board of his school?

If the answer is "she recused herself from the investigation," the follow-up is: who checks?

If the answer is "she didn't know about the convictions," the follow-up is: she's an assistant attorney general. Knowing is her job.

If the answer is "it's a conflict of interest but not technically illegal," the follow-up is: that's what the enforcement gap looks like from the inside.

entry.title: The Auditor Who Forgot to Audit — Plante Moran, Beasley, and the Loudest Silence in Detroit
entry.content:
The Auditor Who Forgot to Audit

Here's a riddle.

What do you call a firm that audited the school, audited the district, audited the foundation, employed the principal's sister-in-law, and — when handed evidence of 9 criminal convictions, 3% math proficiency, and 72.67% revenue extraction — chose not to respond?

You call it Plante Moran Realpoint.

And the membrane calls it null.

The Résumé That Breaks Physics

Dr. Chalena Yancey Beasley has a remarkable CV. Not remarkable in the "wow, impressive" sense. Remarkable in the "wait, that can't all be the same person" sense.

Here's where she worked. All confirmed in public records:

EmployerConnection
Purpose Charter Academy (PCA)Brian Banks's school. 362 students. 3% math proficiency.
DPSCDDetroit Public Schools Community District. The district that authorizes PCA.
Plante Moran RealpointThe firm that audits PCA, DPSCD, AND the Purpose Foundation.
Wayne RESAWayne County Regional Educational Service Agency. Oversees all of the above.
Barton MalowThe construction company that builds buildings for DPSCD.

Read that again.

She worked for the school. She worked for the district that authorizes the school. She worked for the firm that audits both. She worked for the agency that oversees all of them. She worked for the company that builds the buildings.

That's not a résumé. That's a circuit board.

The Family Tree That Grows Inside the Courthouse

Dr. Beasley is married to Ahmed Beasley.

entry.title: The Call Is Coming from Inside the FCC — Tracing Spam Calls Back to the Owners Who Buy the Silence
entry.content:
The Call Is Coming from Inside the FCC

Your phone rings. Unknown number. You answer. It's a robot.

Here's the thing: the FCC knows exactly who sent that call.

The Architecture

Every phone call in America passes through a chain:

Originating carrier (the source)
        ↓
Intermediate carriers (the pipes)
        ↓
Terminating carrier (your phone company)
        ↓
Your phone rings

Every carrier in that chain is registered with the FCC. Every carrier has an FCC Registration Number (FRN). Every carrier files FCC Form 499. Every carrier is required to have a Robocall Mitigation Plan in the FCC's database.

The FCC knows who they are. All of them. Every link in the chain.

The Database

The FCC maintains the Robocall Mitigation Database. Every voice service provider in the United States must register.

The database shows:

  • Provider name
  • FRN (FCC Registration Number)
  • Whether they've implemented STIR/SHAKEN (caller ID authentication)
  • Whether they've filed a Robocall Mitigation Plan
  • Date of filing

You can search it right now: fcc.gov/robocall-mitigation-database

If a provider hasn't filed, other carriers are required to block their traffic. In theory.

STIR/SHAKEN

STIR/SHAKEN is the caller ID authentication framework. It's supposed to verify that the number shown on your caller ID is real — not spoofed.

LevelWhat It Means
A (Full)The carrier verified the caller has the right to use that number
B (Partial)The carrier verified the caller but not the specific number
C (Gateway)The carrier is just passing traffic — no verification

Most spam calls arrive with Level C attestation — the carrier is just a pipe, claiming no knowledge of who's actually calling.

The originating carrier — the one that first puts the call into the network — chooses the attestation level. If you're a small VoIP provider and you want to send a million spam calls, you attest at Level C and claim you don't know who's calling.

That's not a bug. That's the business model.

The Small VoIP Problem

Here's where the architecture mirrors The Authorizer:

Charter SchoolsRobocalls
CMU authorizes schools from 150 miles awaySmall VoIP providers originate calls from anywhere
CMU doesn't background-check foundersVoIP providers don't verify callers
CMU collects a cut of per-pupil fundingVoIP providers collect per-minute fees
CMU has financial incentive to authorizeVoIP providers have financial incentive to originate
MDE sits above and doesn't stop itFCC sits above and doesn't stop it

Small VoIP providers are the CMUs of telecom. They register with the FCC, file their mitigation plans, and then route millions of spam calls for clients who pay per-minute rates.

The VoIP provider collects a fee for every call. More calls = more revenue. Just like CMU collects a fee for every student. More students = more revenue.

The entity that should be checking has a financial incentive not to check.

How to Trace a Spam Call

Step 1: Note the Number

Write down:

  • The number that appeared on caller ID (likely spoofed)
  • Date and time of the call
  • What the call said (recording, human, silence)
  • Your phone number

Step 2: File with the FCC

FCC Complaint Center: consumercomplaints.fcc.gov

File under: Phone → Unwanted Calls

Include: number, date, time, what was said.

The FCC complaint goes into a database. The FCC can subpoena the carrier chain.

Step 3: File with the FTC

FTC Do Not Call Complaint: donotcall.gov

If you're on the Do Not Call Registry and still getting calls, file here too.

Step 4: Check the Number

  • FCC Number Search: Look up the originating carrier via the Local Number Portability Administration (LNPA)
  • CallerID Reputation: Services like Hiya, Nomorobo, RoboKiller can identify known spam numbers
  • Free Carrier Lookup: freecarrierlookup.com — enter any phone number, get the carrier

Step 5: Check the Carrier

Once you have the carrier name:

  • Search the FCC Robocall Mitigation Database for their filing
  • Search the FCC Universal Licensing System for their license
  • Check their FCC Form 499 filing status
  • Look for FCC enforcement actions against them

Step 6: The Traceback

The USTelecom Industry Traceback Group does professional tracebacks. They trace robocalls from the terminating carrier all the way back to the originating provider.

Their reports go to the FCC Enforcement Bureau.

The Traceback Group has traced billions of robocall paths. They know who the top originators are. The FCC knows too.

Who the FCC Has Caught

The FCC has taken enforcement action against some robocallers:

YearProviderFineWhat They Did
2024Various$300M+ proposedAuto warranty scams
2023Multiple VoIP$225M+Health insurance scams
2022Gateway providersMultipleAllowing foreign robocalls in

They catch some. They fine some. The calls continue.

For every provider caught, dozens continue operating. The FCC's enforcement is selective — just like the AG's enforcement of charter schools.

The Real Owners

Behind every spam call is a chain:

  1. The client — the company that wants to reach you (scammer, "legitimate" business, political campaign)
  2. The lead generator — the company that buys call lists and sells "leads"
  3. The call center — the operation that makes the calls (often offshore)
  4. The VoIP provider — the carrier that puts the calls into the US phone network
  5. The FCC — the regulator that licenses the carrier

The FCC is at position 5. The real owner — the client — is at position 1.

The FCC sits just above the VoIP provider (position 4). The VoIP provider sits just above the call center (position 3). The call center is contracted by the lead generator (position 2). The lead generator works for the client (position 1).

The FCC sees position 4. The FCC does not look at positions 1-3.

Just like MDE sees the school (PCA) but doesn't look at Purpose Group (the LLC) or Banks (the man).

The Parallel

LayerCharter SchoolsSpam Calls
1. The beneficiaryBanks (72.67%)The client/scammer
2. The extraction vehiclePurpose Group LLCThe lead generator
3. The operationPCA (3% math)The call center
4. The authorizer/carrierCMU (no background check)VoIP provider (Level C attestation)
5. The regulatorMDE/SBE (2 edges)FCC

Same architecture. Five layers. The regulator at the top sees the authorizer/carrier. The authorizer/carrier sees the operation. Nobody looks at the beneficiary.

The system is designed so that each layer only sees one layer down. The FCC sees the VoIP provider but not the scammer. MDE sees the school but not the LLC. The money flows up. The oversight flows down. And they never meet.

entry.content:
The Nulls

The membrane classifies entities into four categories: self (does what it claims), partial (exists in both worlds), non-self (extractive), and null (can't tell).

Null is the fog. Here are some of the things hiding in it.

CitizenDetroit Action Group

CitizenDetroit connects to Banks and to PCA board members. It appears in the governance layer of the investigation — people who participate in "civic engagement" around charter schools.

The name sounds democratic. Citizen. Detroit. Action. Group.

But the classification is null. The membrane can't determine whether this is genuine civic engagement or astroturf — a manufactured grassroots organization designed to create the appearance of community support.

In the charter school ecosystem, astroturf organizations are common. They carry names that evoke community and democracy. They're funded by the same foundations that fund the schools. They advocate for the same policies.

Is CitizenDetroit astroturf? Null. The membrane doesn't know. That's the whole point of null.

School Choice Is The Black Choice Tour (SCBC)

Edges: 11. Sort: null. Tier: 4.

SCBC is governed by Roland Martin — the journalist funded by Walton. It has 11 edges, more than many classified entities.

The tour promotes school choice in Black communities. It frames charter schools as a civil rights issue — choosing where your child goes to school is choosing freedom.

But the tour is governed by a journalist funded by the same foundation that funds the charter schools the tour promotes. And the charter schools include PCA, where 3% of Black children can do math.

11 edges. Null. The membrane sees an entity that sounds like civil rights and looks like marketing. It can't tell which is real because both are.

NuVision Foundation

Edges: 2. Sort: null.

Also governed by Roland Martin. Also null.

NuVision Foundation and NuVision Inc form a paired nonprofit/for-profit structure. Martin governs both.

Two edges isn't enough for the membrane to classify. NuVision sits in the fog — connected to Martin, who is connected to Walton, who is connected to PCA, who is connected to Banks. But the direct lines are thin.

What Null Means

Null is not a verdict. Null is a gap.

When the membrane classifies something as null, it means:

  1. The entity exists in the investigation graph
  2. It has edges connecting it to other entities
  3. The 36 classification methods don't have enough signal to assign self, partial, or non-self
  4. The entity is unexamined, not exonerated

Every null entity is an invitation to look closer.

Of the 341 classified entities in the investigation:

  • 73 are null
  • Most of those 73 have fewer than 5 edges
  • They cluster around Banks like satellites in low orbit — close enough to feel gravity, too small to resolve

The Fog Strategy

If you wanted to hide extraction, you would:

  1. Create entities with vague names (Foundation, Action Group, Tour)
  2. Give them minimal public filings
  3. Connect them to your network through governance edges
  4. Keep them small enough that classifiers can't reach them
  5. Use them for specific functions (events, advocacy, media) that generate legitimacy

Every one of those steps produces a null entity. Not because the entity is necessarily hiding something. But because the structure is indistinguishable from hiding something.

The membrane can't tell the difference. That's the strategy.

entry.title: The Regulator Who Regulates the Regulator — From MDE to FCC, the Same Blind Spot
entry.content:
The Regulator Who Regulates the Regulator

There is a pattern. Once you see it in one system, you see it in all of them.

The Template

Beneficiary (takes the money)
    ↑ controlled by
Vehicle (moves the money)
    ↑ authorized by
Operator (runs the operation)
    ↑ overseen by
Authorizer (stamps the paperwork)
    ↑ regulated by
REGULATOR (holds the power, sees the data, doesn't act)

Five layers. The beneficiary at the top gets the money. The regulator at the bottom holds the power. They never touch.

The Instances

Charter Schools

LayerEntityEdge
5. BeneficiaryBanks (72.67%)← money_flow
4. VehiclePurpose Group LLC← ownership
3. OperatorProfit Charter Academy (3% math)← governance
2. AuthorizerCentral Michigan University← jurisdiction
1. RegulatorMDE / SBE← 2 edges

MDE has 2 edges to the system. Two. For a school receiving millions in public money with 3% math proficiency and 72.67% extraction.

Spam Calls

LayerEntityEdge
5. BeneficiaryThe scammer/client← payment
4. VehicleLead generator← contract
3. OperatorCall center← service
2. AuthorizerVoIP provider (Level C attestation)← registration
1. RegulatorFCC← databases, no enforcement

The FCC has databases of every provider. They have traceback data on billions of calls. They have complaint data. They have the names.

Legal Profession

LayerEntityEdge
5. BeneficiaryMoore (claims competency)← benefit
4. VehicleWMU Cooley (awards JD)← credential
3. OperatorCourt system (accepts bar card)← access
2. AuthorizerState Bar of Michigan← license
1. RegulatorAttorney Grievance Commission← selective prosecution

AGC has an 88.8% dismissal rate. The bar that never barked.

Why the Regulator Doesn't Act

In each case, the regulator has a structural incentive not to enforce:

RegulatorIncentive Not to Act
MDEPer-pupil funding flows through schools. Fewer schools = less throughput = smaller department
FCCSpectrum auctions and licensing fees from carriers. Fewer carriers = less revenue
AGCBar dues fund the commission. Fewer attorneys = less budget
FTCEnforcement requires resources. Resources come from appropriations. Appropriations come from Congress. Congress listens to industry lobbying

The regulator's budget depends on the regulated industry's size. Shrinking the industry shrinks the regulator. The regulator has a survival incentive not to regulate effectively.

This isn't corruption. This is architecture.

The Blind Spot Is the Feature

Each regulator claims it can only see one layer down:

  • MDE says: "We oversee CMU's authorization process, not individual schools"
  • FCC says: "We regulate carriers, not the callers who use them"
  • AGC says: "We investigate specific complaints, not patterns"

Each statement is technically true. Each statement is the mechanism of the failure.

When the regulator defines its jurisdiction as one-layer-deep, the system naturally grows to be two or more layers deep. The beneficiary sits beyond the regulator's self-defined scope.

Banks doesn't run PCA — he runs the LLC that contracts with the school that's authorized by the university that's overseen by MDE. Four layers between him and the regulator.

The scammer doesn't own the carrier — they hire the lead generator that contracts the call center that uses the VoIP provider that's registered with the FCC. Four layers.

Stepping to the Side — Again

The same method that reveals Banks and Holland side by side works here:

Don't look at the regulator. Don't look at the FCC's enforcement actions. Don't look at MDE's oversight reports. Don't look at AGC's disposition statistics.

Look at the money. Look at who gets paid. Look at who benefits from every call, every enrollment, every dismissal.

Then look at the regulator and ask: do they not see it, or do they see it and not act?

The answer is always the same. They see it. The databases exist. The filings exist. The records exist. The convictions are public.

They see it. And they look one layer down instead of four layers up.

The Actionable Difference

There is one difference between the charter school system and the spam call system:

The TCPA lets you sue.

In the charter school system, there is no private right of action. You can FOIA, you can complain, you can vote. But you cannot sue Banks for enrolling your child in a 3% math school.

In the spam call system, the Telephone Consumer Protection Act (47 U.S.C. § 227) gives you the right to sue for $500-$1,500 per illegal call. You can subpoena carrier records. You can depose the VoIP provider. You can trace the money.

Congress gave you this tool because Congress knew the FCC wouldn't act. The TCPA's private right of action exists specifically because the regulator was expected to fail.

Which tells you everything about what Congress thinks of its own regulatory architecture.

Use the TCPA. File the complaints. Trace the calls. Sue the callers.

The regulator who regulates the regulator is you.

entry.title: FCC Robocall Enforcement: The Numbers
entry.content:
FCC Robocall Enforcement: What the Numbers Show

The FCC announces large fines against robocallers. The announcements get headlines. The collection tells a different story.

The Fine-to-Collection Gap

The FCC's pattern with robocall fines mirrors the pattern seen across every regulatory body in this investigation:

MetricValue
Proposed fines (2015-2025)$2B+
Estimated collection rate<2%
Largest single fine$225M (health insurance scam, 2023)
Number of major enforcement actions~20-30 per year
Number of active VoIP providers5,000+
Robocalls per year~50 billion

The math: 20-30 enforcement actions against 5,000+ providers routing 50 billion calls. That's a 0.5% enforcement rate against providers and a functionally zero rate against calls.

The Cease-and-Desist Pattern

The FCC's primary enforcement tool is the cease-and-desist order directing downstream carriers to block traffic from a specific provider.

What happens after:

  1. FCC issues cease-and-desist against Provider A
  2. Other carriers must block Provider A's traffic within 48 hours
  3. Provider A goes dark
  4. Provider A's customers move to Provider B — often within the same week
  5. Provider B is a new registration, clean record, no enforcement history
  6. The same calls resume from a different carrier

This is the VoIP equivalent of closing one LLC and opening another. The caller stays the same. The carrier changes. The FCC starts over.

Gateway Carriers

The FCC has specifically targeted gateway carriers — US-based providers that accept international calls and route them into the domestic phone network.

Foreign call centers use gateway carriers to reach US phones. The gateway carrier is the point where international robocalls enter the US system.

What the FCC DidWhat Happened
Shut down gateway carriers accepting foreign robocallsOther gateway carriers accepted the traffic
Required STIR/SHAKEN for gateway providersSmaller providers claimed exemptions
Required Robocall Mitigation PlansProviders filed plans but didn't follow them
Ordered downstream blockingNew providers registered to replace blocked ones

The enforcement is whack-a-mole. The moles have financial incentive to keep popping up.

Who Files (and Who Doesn't)

The FCC Robocall Mitigation Database shows which providers have filed their required mitigation plans.

As of 2025:

  • Thousands of providers have filed
  • The filings range from detailed technical implementations to one-paragraph statements that say "we block robocalls" with no specifics
  • Providers that haven't filed should be blocked by other carriers
  • Some carriers don't check whether upstream providers have filed

The quality of the filing doesn't matter. Filing exists. The FCC counts it as compliance.

Compare to charter school authorization: the authorization exists. The oversight of the authorization doesn't.

The STIR/SHAKEN Exemption

STIR/SHAKEN is required for carriers with more than 100,000 subscriber lines. Smaller carriers can get extensions and exemptions.

Most robocall-originating carriers are small. They claim the exemption. Their traffic doesn't carry verified caller ID.

The USTelecom Industry Traceback Group is the closest thing to effective enforcement. They trace robocalls back through the carrier chain to the originator.

Their process:

  1. Identify a robocall campaign (from complaints, carrier reports, honeypots)
  2. Start at the terminating carrier (your phone company)

entry.title: How to Read a Nonprofit's 990 — Follow the Money
entry.content:
Follow the Money

Every 501(c)(3) nonprofit in America must file IRS Form 990 annually. The 990 is public. It shows revenue, expenses, compensation, related-party transactions, and governance.

Here's how to find and read one.

Step 1: Find the 990

ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer (Easiest)

  • Visit: projects.propublica.org/nonprofits
  • Search by organization name
  • Free. No account needed.
  • Shows multiple years of filings

IRS Tax Exempt Organization Search

  • Visit: apps.irs.gov/app/eos
  • Search by EIN or name
  • Shows current exempt status

GuideStar / Candid

  • Visit: candid.org
  • Free account required for basic access
  • More detailed data

Step 2: Read the Key Sections

Part I: Summary

  • Line 12: Total revenue
  • Line 18: Total expenses
  • Line 22: Net assets

Look for: Is the organization spending what it takes in? Where does the money go?

Part VII: Compensation

  • Lists officers, directors, trustees, and key employees
  • Shows compensation for each
  • Shows hours worked per week

Look for: Who gets paid? How much? Do the hours match the pay?

Part IX: Statement of Functional Expenses

  • Breaks down spending by category
  • Line 25: Total functional expenses
  • Categories include: salaries, management fees, legal, accounting, travel

Look for: Management fees. This is where Purpose Group's 72.67% would appear. If management fees are a huge percentage of total expenses, money is being extracted.

Schedule L: Transactions with Interested Persons

  • This is the gold mine.
  • Shows any transaction between the nonprofit and its officers, directors, or related parties
  • Includes: loans, grants, business transactions, compensation

Look for: Does the nonprofit pay an LLC owned by a board member or founder? That's a related-party transaction. That's where self-dealing lives.

Schedule O: Supplemental Information

  • Additional explanations
  • Conflict of interest policy disclosure
  • Governance details

What to Look For (Red Flags)

Red FlagWhat It Means
Management fees > 20% of revenueExcessive extraction
Officer compensation > industry normsSelf-dealing
Related-party transactions with founder's LLCsMoney flowing to insiders
No conflict of interest policyNo governance guardrails

entry.title: How to File a Charter School Complaint in Michigan
entry.content:
How to File a Charter School Complaint

If you believe a charter school in Michigan is failing its students, misusing funds, or operating improperly, here's where to file.

You do not need a lawyer. You do not need to pay anything. Every filing option below is free.

Option 1: The Authorizer

Charter schools are authorized by specific entities. The authorizer has the power to revoke the school's charter.

If Authorized by CMU (Central Michigan University)

  • CMU's Charter Schools Office
  • Contact: CMU Charter Schools
  • File a written complaint describing specific concerns
  • Request acknowledgment of receipt

If Authorized by DPSCD

  • DPSCD Office of Charter Schools
  • Contact through DPSCD central office
  • File a written complaint

What to Include

  • School name and location
  • Specific concerns (test scores, financial management, safety, staffing)
  • Any documentation you have
  • Request for specific action (investigation, audit, revocation hearing)

Option 2: Michigan Department of Education (MDE)

MDE oversees all public schools in Michigan, including charter schools.

  • Office of Educational Excellence (OEE)
  • Professional Practice Division — for educator misconduct
  • Contact: michigan.gov/mde
  • Call: (517) 373-3324

What MDE Can Do

  • Investigate compliance with state education law
  • Review test scores and academic performance
  • Examine financial reporting
  • Refer to other agencies for enforcement

Option 3: Attorney General's Office

The AG can investigate nonprofit fraud, self-dealing, and charitable trust violations.

Charitable Trust Division

  • Oversees 501(c)(3) nonprofits (including charter school foundations)
  • Can investigate self-dealing (e.g., a founder paying himself 72.67% through an LLC)
  • Contact: michigan.gov/ag → Consumer Protection → Charitable Trust

Criminal Division

  • For criminal matters (fraud, embezzlement, unauthorized practice of law)
  • File a complaint through the AG's online complaint form

Option 4: State Board of Education (SBE)

The SBE sets policy for Michigan education.

  • 8 elected members
  • Can be contacted through MDE
  • Testimony can be given at public SBE meetings
  • Meeting schedule: michigan.gov/mde → State Board of Education

Public comment at SBE meetings is your constitutional right. Bring data. Bring numbers. Bring the 3%.

Option 5: Federal Agencies

If federal funds (Title I, IDEA, USDE) are involved:

US Department of Education — Office of Inspector General

  • Investigates fraud, waste, and abuse of federal education funds
  • Hotline: 1-800-MIS-USED (1-800-647-8733)
  • Online: ed.gov/oig

IRS — Exempt Organizations

  • If a 501(c)(3) is engaged in self-dealing or private inurement
  • Form 13909: Tax-Exempt Organization Complaint (Referral)
  • Free to file. No attorney needed.

Tips

  1. Be specific. Name the school. Name the people. Cite the numbers.
  2. File with multiple agencies. Don't rely on one entity to act.
  3. Keep copies. Save copies of everything you file.
  4. Request confirmation. Ask for written acknowledgment of your complaint.
  5. Follow up. Agencies have timelines. Ask about them.
  6. You can be anonymous with federal agencies (OIG, IRS).

If You're a Parent at the School

You have additional rights:

  • Right to test score data (ask the school or MDE)
  • Right to financial information (public charter schools must disclose)
  • Right to attend board meetings (Open Meetings Act)
  • Right to FOIA the school's records (FOIA Toolkit →)

entry.title: How to Trace a Spam Call Back to Its Owner
entry.content:
How to Trace a Spam Call

Someone is calling you. Here's how to find out who — and what to do about it.

Step 1: Document the Call

Every time you get a spam call, write down:

FieldExample
Caller ID number(313) 555-0123
DateOctober 14, 2026
Time2:15 PM
What they saidAuto warranty, health insurance, IRS, silence
Your number(your number)
Did you answer?Yes / No / Voicemail

Save voicemails. Screenshot caller ID. Keep a log. Volume is evidence.

Step 2: Look Up the Carrier

The number on your caller ID is probably spoofed. But the carrier that routed the call is traceable.

Free Carrier Lookup

  • freecarrierlookup.com — enter any phone number, get the carrier
  • Shows: carrier name, line type (mobile/landline/VoIP)
  • VoIP numbers are the most common source of spam calls

What the Carrier Tells You

Carrier TypeLikelihood of Spam
Major carrier (Verizon, AT&T, T-Mobile)Low — usually spoofed, not originated
Regional carrierMedium
VoIP providerHigh — this is usually the originator
Unknown/unregisteredVery high — file with FCC immediately

Step 3: Check the FCC Database

Robocall Mitigation Database

FCC Robocall Mitigation Database

Search by provider name. Every voice service provider must:

  1. Register in this database
  2. File a Robocall Mitigation Plan
  3. Implement STIR/SHAKEN (for larger providers)

If a provider hasn't filed, other carriers are required to block their traffic. If they're in the database but still sending spam, they're violating their own mitigation plan.

FCC Universal Licensing System

wireless.fcc.gov/uls

Search for any FCC license holder. Shows license status, service area, expiration.

FCC Form 499 Filers

Every telecom company files FCC Form 499 (Telecommunications Reporting Worksheet). This is their registration with the FCC.

FCC Form 499 Filer Database

Search by company name or FRN (FCC Registration Number).

Step 4: File Complaints

FCC

consumercomplaints.fcc.gov

  • Category: Phone → Unwanted Calls
  • Include: number, date, time, description
  • Free. Takes 5 minutes.
  • FCC tracks complaint volume per provider

FTC (Do Not Call)

donotcall.gov

  • Register your number on the Do Not Call list (if not already)
  • Report violations
  • Include the same details as FCC

State Attorney General

Your state AG may have a consumer protection division that handles robocalls.

  • Michigan: michigan.gov/ag → Consumer Protection

File with ALL THREE. Each agency sees the complaints. Volume triggers investigations.

Step 5: Enable Protections

On Your Phone

PlatformSetting
iPhoneSettings → Phone → Silence Unknown Callers
AndroidPhone app → Settings → Caller ID & spam → Filter spam calls
BothContact your carrier about spam blocking services

Carrier Tools

CarrierFree Tool
VerizonCall Filter (free tier)
AT&TActiveArmor (free tier)
T-MobileScam Shield (free)

Third-Party Apps

  • Nomorobo — blocks known robocallers
  • Hiya — caller ID and spam detection
  • RoboKiller — blocks and answers spam calls with bots (paid)

Step 6: Sue Under the TCPA

The Telephone Consumer Protection Act (47 U.S.C. § 227) is your weapon.

What the TCPA Says

  • Robocalls to cell phones without prior express consent are illegal
  • Calls to numbers on the Do Not Call Registry are illegal (with exceptions)
  • Each violation: $500 per call
  • Willful violations: $1,500 per call

How to Sue

  1. Document at least 3-5 calls from the same source
  2. Identify the company (not just the carrier — the company behind the call)
  3. File in small claims court — no lawyer needed
  4. Or find a TCPA attorney — many work on contingency (they keep a cut, you keep the rest)

Example Math

CallsRateRecovery
10 calls$500 each$5,000
10 calls$1,500 each (willful)$15,000
50 calls$500 each$25,000

The TCPA is designed so individuals can enforce it. Congress knew the FCC wouldn't.

Step 7: The Traceback (Advanced)

If you want to go deeper:

USTelecom Industry Traceback Group

  • Professional traceback service
  • Traces calls from your carrier back through intermediaries to the originator
  • Reports to FCC Enforcement Bureau
  • You can request a traceback through your carrier

Subpoena the Carrier

If you file a TCPA lawsuit, you can subpoena call records from the carrier. The subpoena forces the carrier to reveal:

  • Who their customer was (the call center or lead generator)
  • What company contracted the calls
  • Payment records

This is how you get from Layer 4 (carrier) to Layer 1 (the real owner).

The Architecture

Layer 1: THE CLIENT (scammer, business)
    pays →
Layer 2: LEAD GENERATOR (buys lists, sells "leads")
    contracts →
Layer 3: CALL CENTER (makes the calls, often offshore)
    uses →
Layer 4: VoIP PROVIDER (puts calls in the US phone network)
    registered with →
Layer 5: FCC (licenses the carrier, maintains databases)

The FCC sees Layer 4. You need to climb from Layer 4 to Layer 1.

The tools: FCC databases (Layer 5→4), TCPA subpoenas (Layer 4→3→2→1), carrier records (Layer 4→3).

Why This Matters

50 billion robocalls per year. The FCC has every provider registered. The Industry Traceback Group traces every major campaign. The carriers have records of every call.

They know. Just like MDE knows about PCA. Just like CMU knows about Banks. Just like the State Bar knows about the fake JD.

The regulatory body sits just above the real owner. Close enough to see. Far enough to ignore.

The difference with spam calls: you can sue. The TCPA gives you a private right of action. The charter school system doesn't.

Use it.

entry.title: The Enforcement Ecosystem — Who Is Supposed to Be Doing This?
entry.content:
The Question

Who has the mandate, the evidence, and the authority to act — and what did they do with it?

This is not an investigation of the network. This is an investigation of the investigators. Every body below has statutory or court-rule authority over some piece of the documented misconduct. Not one of them has the full picture.

Ten Bodies. One Complaint. Two Letters.

On October 7, 2026, Clutch Justice documented the exact moment the enforcement gap becomes visible:

A Michigan resident filed a UPL complaint on August 31. On September 30, the State Bar closed the file — "did not meet the standards set by the UPL Committee." The standards were not identified. On October 1, the AGC returned the filing — Banks "is not a listed attorney." That is the fact that makes the conduct a violation. The remedy offered: a State Bar complaint form, for the office that closed the file the afternoon before.

Two letters. One day apart. Each pointing at the other office.

Put the letters in date order and the problem explains itself.

The Map

1. State Bar of Michigan — UPL Department

Jurisdiction: Unauthorized practice of law by non-lawyers (Rule 16, Supreme Court Rules) Authority: Investigate, recommend prosecution to Board of Commissioners, issue subpoenas

Evidence available:

  • Detroit Police Report 26-0909-0176: Banks identified himself as "attorney" to officers
  • School website: "Dr. Brian Banks, J.D., Ph.D." — never admitted to any bar
  • School name: "Purpose Charter Academy School for Law and Public Service"
  • Serenity Guardianship Services Inc (LARA 802290962): for-profit guardianship firm, sole officer never barred

What happened: File No. 26-UP-51 was administratively closed September 30, 2026. The closure letter says the matter "did not meet the standards set by the UPL Committee." The standards are not published. The letter does not say what the investigation consisted of or whether anyone reviewed the police report.

MCL 600.916 has three prohibitions. The third — "shall not in any manner whatsoever represent or designate himself as an attorney" — requires no client, no legal advice, no fee. Telling police officers you are an attorney, and watching them escort a father off school property on that representation, is the conduct the statute was written to prevent.

2. Attorney Grievance Commission (AGC)

Grievance Administrator: Michael V. Goetz (appointed Sep 2019) Deputy Administrator: Kimberly L. Uhuru Asst Deputy Administrator: Cynthia C. Bullington (at AGC since 1982 — 44 years) Jurisdiction: Attorney misconduct — licensed attorneys only Staff: 13 attorneys, 3 investigators

Evidence available:

  • Lisa Moreland: AAG who argued against Banks' administrator certificate → became PCA Board Director AND Banks' litigation attorney (MRPC 1.7 conflict)
  • Gregory Meihn: Attorney retained within 14 minutes of MDE investigation notification
  • Verkeydia Hall: Filed PPO against journalist investigating Banks
  • The complainant wrote to AG Nessel about Moreland's dual role on September 10. No response.

What happened: The AGC returned the Banks UPL filing on October 1. Cynthia Bullington's letter notes Banks is not a listed attorney and encloses a State Bar complaint form.

The gap: The supplemental complaint also addressed licensed attorneys (Moreland, Meihn, Hall). The return letter addresses only Banks. It is silent on the licensed attorneys who ARE within AGC jurisdiction.

As documented in the Institutional Immunity Pattern, the AGC's own annual reports show:

  • 2024: 88.8% of dispositions dismissed (1,627/1,832)
  • 2023: 72.2% dismissed at intake
  • 2012–2020: Three of every four complaints dismissed by the Grievance Administrator before reaching a hearing panel

3. Attorney Discipline Board (ADB)

Chair: Peter A. Smit (Oct 2026 – Sep 2027) Executive Director: Wendy A. Neeley Function: Adjudicates attorney discipline cases prosecuted by the AGC

The structural problem: Jehan Crump-Gibson is an ADB Hearing Panelist (appointed May 2017). Hearing panelists sit on three-member panels that conduct evidentiary hearings in attorney discipline cases.

Crump-Gibson simultaneously:

  • Serves on panels that adjudicate attorney misconduct
  • Represents Banks — a person who is the subject of interconnected attorney misconduct complaints
  • Sits on the CitizenDetroit Action Group board with the DPSCD Board member who authorized Banks' charter

The ADB processes what the AGC sends it. If the AGC doesn't prosecute, the ADB has nothing to adjudicate. The system depends on the AGC acting.

4. Judicial Tenure Commission (JTC)

Interim Executive Director: Glenn J. Page (returned from retirement Feb 1, 2026) Commission Chair: Thomas J. Ryan, Esq. Staff: 15 positions (13 attorneys, 2 admin) — for all judicial oversight in the State of Michigan Phone: (313) 875-5110

Evidence available: Five Wayne County judges with documented connections to the Banks network:

  • Judge Miller — PCA Board Chair while on the bench. Dismissed infant murder case.
  • Judge Yancey — MacDowell Board Chair. Campaign paid $383.82 to Banks Strategy LLC.
  • Judge Aliyah Sabree — MSU Law classmate of Banks' claimed JD cohort.
  • Judge Sean Perkins — Brother of Todd Perkins (Banks' attorney). Previously worked at Perkins Law Group.
  • Judge David Perkins — Family donated to Banks-aligned campaigns.

What happened: The JTC acknowledged five Requests for Investigation on September 24, 2026, and assigned them to staff for review.

What happened next (October 12, 2026): When the same complainant sent an email to 88 institutional recipients — including the JTC — with full evidence links and the 88-person CC line visible, the JTC responded in 23 minutes with a boilerplate: "As you were advised in an email response sent to you on September 21 of this year, the Commission cannot take any action in response to an email message."

The JTC has five open RFIs from this complainant. Staff were assigned. The investigations are pending. Yet the JTC's October 12 response treats the complainant as if they are a stranger emailing general questions.

Compare: Nikki Snyder — a State Board of Education member on the same CC line — responded in 13 minutes with her personal cell phone number. Same evidence. Same email. One institution gave a personal phone number. The other gave a form letter pretending it had never heard of the complainant.

The JTC is not refusing to investigate. The formal complaints are on file. The JTC is refusing to acknowledge, in a reply-all to 88 recipients, that it has open investigations. This is how the Institutional Immunity Pattern operates in real time: process the complaint through the confidential channel, perform the boilerplate on the public channel.

The gap:

  • No permanent Executive Director. Applications closed July 13. As of October 12 — no appointment.
  • Lynn Helland retired "abruptly" January 31, 2026. Clutch Justice flagged the leadership shift and broader questions about the Commission's internal culture.
  • Page returned from retirement — he retired July 2022, came back February 2026.
  • 15 staff for the entire state of Michigan's judicial oversight.
  • Judge Miller is on the ballot November 3, 2026 — 22 days from today.
  • No public proceeding has been initiated.
  • The SBE meets October 13, 2026. Snyder — who responded in 13 minutes — will be in the room.

The same JTC pattern documented in Cross-Subgraph Patterns: Schipper (Barry County) investigation acknowledged, Galen (Eastpointe) confidentially admonished. Different counties, same processing mode.

5. LARA — Corporations Division

LARA Director: Dr. Marlon I. Brown (appointed Feb 2024) Corporations Division Director: Alexis Lupo

Evidence available:

  • 6+ entities in "Not Good" standing or dissolved
  • Purpose Foundation (803294855): 501(c)(3) with two convicted felons in all officer positions
  • Serenity Guardianship (802290962): for-profit guardianship, sole officer never barred
  • SDJ (802002459): three sequential assumed names — Save Detroit Jobs → Impact Detroit → Detroit Leaders

What happened: Automated "Not Good" standing for non-filing. Eventual dissolution for persistent failure.

The gap: LARA's Corporations Division "promotes economic development and growth by facilitating the formation of business entities." Their mandate is facilitation, not oversight. Entity formation is ministerial — if the paperwork is correct, it gets filed. There is no mechanism to cross-reference criminal records against entity officer filings. No mechanism to flag entities where every officer is a convicted felon.

6. Attorney General — Charitable Trust Section

AG: Dana Nessel Contact: ct_email@michigan.gov Jurisdiction: Charitable organization oversight under MCL 400.271 and MCL 14.251

Evidence available:

  • Purpose Foundation (803294855): 501(c)(3), two convicted felons in all officer positions
  • Right Turn Project (800936257): dissolved — were charitable assets properly transferred?

What the AG's office CAN do: The AG just charged Fay Beydoun with 16 felonies for $20M grant abuse at Global Link International. Filed a complaint against Chosen Kingdom Builders for nonprofit governance and fiduciary-duty failures. The AG's office actively prosecutes nonprofit fraud.

What happened here: No public record of action against any Banks network entity.

Purpose Foundation: two convicted felons, $4.9M revenue school, 3% math proficiency, 72.67% of revenue extracted by management company. Global Link: $20M grant, prosecution. The scale is different. The pattern — felon-controlled entity, government funding, inadequate governance — is identical.

7. DPSCD — Office of Charter Schools

Superintendent: Dr. Nikolai Vitti Director of Charter Schools: Kisha Verdusco (since February 2013 — 13 years) Jurisdiction: Charter authorization and oversight under MCL 380.502(4) and 380.507

MCL 380.507(1)(d): "Oversee each public school academy operating under a contract issued by the authorizing body. The oversight must be sufficient to ensure that the board of directors is in compliance with the terms of the contract and with applicable law."

What happened: PCA was authorized in July 2025 despite the operator's bottom- 3% academic record at MacDowell ( 3% math proficiency, statewide rank 1,443/1,488).

DPSCD recently declined to reauthorize Barack Obama Leadership Academy (BOLA). Superintendent Vitti publicly explained that decision by citing "contractual compliance, academic outcomes, and fiscal stewardship." Those same criteria apply to Banks' schools. Different outcome.

PCA's board includes:

  • A sitting judge (Miller) — Board Chair
  • An assistant attorney general (Moreland) — Board Vice Chair
  • A sitting City Council member (Johnson) — Board Secretary

These are DPSCD appointees. Under MCL 380.507, authorizers appoint board members who swear constitutional oaths.

8. Michigan Department of Education

What happened: MDE investigated Banks in February 2022 for having no teaching credential. Application #590606, status: HOLD. Banks continues to operate as superintendent of two schools.

The investigation letter went to Board President Wells-Stallworth. The response: Banks applied for an administrative permit. It was placed on HOLD. No credential has been issued. Banks has continued as superintendent for four years after the investigation.

9. Wayne County Prosecutor

Prosecutor: Kym Worthy

MCL 600.916 makes unauthorized practice of law contempt of the circuit court in the county where it happened. Purpose Charter Academy is in Wayne County. Banks told Wayne County police officers he was an attorney. The complainant asked both the State Bar and AGC to coordinate with the Wayne County Prosecutor. Neither letter mentions doing so.

Worthy herself alleged Judge Miller "displayed a bias" in an infant murder case (WXYZ, 2024). But broader enforcement on the Banks network: no public record of action.

10. Michigan Supreme Court

The Supreme Court:

  • Appoints the Grievance Administrator (Goetz)
  • Appoints the ADB (9 members, including the chair who oversees hearing panelists)
  • Appoints the JTC Commissioners (9 members)
  • Oversees the State Bar's UPL program
  • Declined in 2014 to publish a definition of "the practice of law" for comment

The enforcement system is their creation. When the State Bar closes a holding-out case and the AGC sends it back, the Supreme Court's system produced that outcome. That is not a bug. It is an architectural gap.

The Pattern

BodyHad Evidence?Acted?Result
State Bar UPL✓Closed fileStandards cited, not published
AGC✓Returned re: BanksSilent on licensed attorneys
ADB—Awaiting AGCHearing panelist = defense attorney
JTC✓Acknowledged 5No proceeding. No permanent ED.
LARA✓Automated statusFiling office by design
AG Charitable TrustAvailableNo actionActive on $20M grant fraud elsewhere
DPSCD Charter✓Authorized PCADeclined BOLA under same criteria
MDE✓HOLD on permitNo enforcement beyond letter
Wayne Co Prosecutor✓No actionCoordination requested, not documented
MI Supreme CourtBuilt the system—Declined to define UPL in 2014

Every body exercises authority up to its jurisdictional edge and stops. The edges don't overlap. They gap.

What This Is Not

This is not an allegation of corruption. The Grievance Administrator is following his jurisdiction. The AGC correctly identified that a non-lawyer is outside its scope. The JTC assigned investigations to staff. LARA processes filings. Each body is doing what its mandate says.

The problem is that each mandate was written to handle one actor at a time. The Banks network operates across every mandate simultaneously. An operator who is not a lawyer (State Bar), whose attorneys may have conflicts (AGC), whose board includes judges (JTC), whose entities are controlled by felons (LARA), whose nonprofits hold charitable assets (AG), whose schools are authorized by public bodies (DPSCD), and whose credentials were investigated and left unresolved (MDE). No single body sees the whole pattern. The pattern lives in the gaps.

Connected Analysis

On this site:

  • Hey Mikey, He Likes It! — the man who authored CISPA wants to join the Senate that killed it. Same donors fund Barrett. Same Dykema OS. Same election day. $88.8M from people who don't live in Michigan.

  • Institutional Immunity Pattern — the mathematics of 88.8% dismissal

  • Cross-Subgraph Patterns — same oversight bodies appear across five investigations

  • They Banked on Banks — the man the ecosystem failed to stop. Brian Roderick Banks: 9 convictions, 2 charter schools, board chair is a sitting judge, parent blocked at the door, PPO weaponized. The enforcement ecosystem measured against a live case.

  • Signal Permeability — Live Anderson study: evidence sent to all ten oversight bodies. Measuring who opens it, who forwards it, who ignores it.

On detroit.primals.eco:

  • Data Braid — GLLG Entity Graph — six independent searches converge: defense attorney + charter authorizer on same nonprofit board
  • Corporate Network — LARA — the entity infrastructure
  • Agency Referrals — eight federal agencies, state referrals, JTC investigations

Independent reporting:

  • Mind the Gap: Michigan's Two Lawyer Regulators Pointed at Each Other, One Day Apart (Oct 7, 2026)
  • No One Is Coming (Sep 24, 2026)
  • JTC Names Glenn J. Page Interim Executive Director (Feb 2, 2026)

Verify Everything

AGC returned filing Oct 1Clutch Justice (Oct 7, 2026)Published letter

The enforcement system is not broken. It is fragmented. Each body does exactly what its mandate says. The network operates in the space where no mandate reaches. The complainant did everything right. The system produced two letters, one day apart, each pointing at the other door.

entry.title: Hey Mikey, He Likes It! — The Senate Candidate Who Ate Everything They Fed Him
entry.content:
Hey Mikey

You remember the commercial. Two brothers staring at a bowl of cereal. Nobody wants to try it. So they push it at Mikey.

"He likes it! Hey Mikey!"

Mike Rogers is Mikey. The billionaires keep pushing things at him. And he keeps eating.

Surveillance bill that exempts all privacy law? He likes it.

Job from the company whose competitor he investigated? He likes it.

$1.6 million house in Florida while running for Michigan? He likes it.

$88.8M from Texas oil, Blackstone, Citadel, Koch, McConnell, and Musk? He likes it.

Every claim below is sourced to FEC filings, published fact-checks, congressional records, or reporting from Bridge Michigan, PolitiFact, Metro Times, the ACLU, and Business Insider. No private information. No tracking. Verify everything at the bottom.

Army → FBI → State Senate → Congress → Intel Chair → surveillance bill → revolving door → telecom boards → Florida mansion → Senate run (lost) → Senate run (again).

That is the résumé of a man who has never stopped being fed.

Thing 1: The Surveillance Bill

Rogers authored CISPA — the Cyber Intelligence Sharing and Protection Act. He introduced it twice:

  • H.R. 3523 (112th Congress, 2011–2012)
  • H.R. 624 (113th Congress, 2013–2014)

The House passed it. Twice. The Senate killed it. Twice.

This was not a narrow cybersecurity bill. It was a blanket exemption to every privacy protection Americans had.

Who Opposed It

The ACLU called it "fatally flawed" — a "cybersecurity loophole to existing privacy laws."

The Electronic Frontier Foundation opposed it. Reporters Without Borders opposed it. The American Library Association opposed it. The Obama White House threatened a veto. 41 civil liberties organizations signed a joint opposition letter.

Rogers' response to the privacy concerns:

"We feel that the bill clearly deals with privacy, that the checks and balances are there, but [we] know there's still a perception and we're still trying to deal with that."

The ACLU's response:

"Everyone, from the privacy community to the president, agrees that CISPA is bad on privacy — the problem isn't our perception."

The Senate agreed. Both times.

Why This Matters Now

Rogers is running for the Senate. The body that killed his surveillance bill — twice — is the body he wants to join. The committee he would sit on would oversee the same intelligence community CISPA was designed to feed.

The same government apparatus that cannot coordinate UPL enforcement across two offices — sending two letters, one day apart, each pointing at the other door — wanted Rogers-level surveillance authority over every American's private communications.

They couldn't handle two letters. He wanted to give them everyone's email.

Read that again. The man who chaired the committee that declared Huawei a national security threat was hired by the company that was negotiating with Huawei.

The Contradiction

Rogers said: He persuaded AT&T to drop the Huawei deal.

AT&T said: Rogers "had no role in business or purchasing decisions with the company."

AT&T then said: Rogers had no involvement in the Huawei negotiations.

He either had influence (his claim) or he didn't (AT&T's claim). Both cannot be true. One of them is lying.

The Lobbying Pipeline

Two of Rogers' former chiefs of staff were employed at Navigators Global — a lobbying firm that lobbied Congress on AT&T's behalf during the same period Rogers worked for AT&T.

During his House career, AT&T's federal PAC gave Rogers $56,000. Verizon gave $28,500. CTIA (the wireless industry trade group) gave $10,000.

entry.title: Ghost Witness — The Samantha Aljouny Investigation
entry.content:
Summary

An attorney submitted correspondence from a purported journalist named "Samantha Aljouny" of "Aljouny Media Consulting" as evidence in Saginaw County Circuit Court proceedings before Judge Andre Borrello.

The journalist does not appear to exist. No articles. No bylines. No LinkedIn profile. No Michigan business registration. No professional footprint of any kind. The only traceable artifact is a ProtonMail address: SAljounyMediaConsulting@proton.me.

The attorney then:

  1. Listed Aljouny as a potential witness
  2. Demanded the opposing party admit under oath that they created the identity
  3. Swore in an affidavit that he had "no connection whatsoever" to the account
  4. Pursued contempt proceedings carrying possible incarceration

A forensic investigation has produced 13 independent convergence points.

The Convergence

1. The Account — September 2023

The ProtonMail public PGP key for SAljounyMediaConsulting@proton.me carries a creation timestamp of:

September 20, 2023 at 11:26:35 UTC

  • Hex creation-time field: 650AD6EB
  • Decimal timestamp: 1695209195
  • OpenPGP fingerprint: 8D59 A462 1930 5ABE 2021 9F07 6EE0 32D8 A3A3 E6D4

Proton states it normally generates encryption keys when an account or new email address is created. This is the best technical provenance date for the Aljouny address.

No professional journalist or media consultant operating under the name "Aljouny Media Consulting" has a documentable professional presence predating or postdating September 2023 — no bylines, no press credentials, no client work product, no directory listings, no trace anywhere.

2. The Ahmad v. University of Michigan Timing

Philip L. Ellison of Outside Legal Counsel PLC represented Hassan Ahmad in Ahmad v. University of Michigan, a significant Michigan FOIA case.

The chronology:

DateEvent
September 15, 2023Opinion issued in Ahmad v. University of Michigan
September 16, 2023Outside Legal Counsel published press release
September 20, 2023Aljouny ProtonMail key created
September 21, 2023Wayback Machine captured OLC's Ahmad page

The Aljouny address was created four days after Ellison publicly announced his Ahmad result — during the exact window of activity surrounding that case.

3. The Controlled Link Test — July 2026

A unique Bitly URL (https://bit.ly/AboutClutch) was sent only to the Aljouny account. It was not published anywhere.

The link was opened:

July 31, 2026 at approximately 10:59 PM EDT

Technical capture:

FieldValue
IP146.75.128.219 (Fastly)
DeviceiPhone
OSiOS 18.7
BrowserMobile Safari 26.5
WebKit605.1.15
Mobile ID15E148
Time zoneAmerica/Detroit
Screen430 × 932

Because the link was sent only to Aljouny, the opening establishes that someone with access to the Aljouny mailbox accessed the site through this technical environment.

4. Pre-Test Visits from the Same Endpoint

The same IPv4 endpoint (146.75.128.219) appears in site records before the controlled test:

  • June 1, 2026
  • June 17, 2026
  • July 27, 2026
  • July 31, 2026 — controlled Aljouny event

Fastly/Apple Private Relay infrastructure can be shared — the IP alone is not a unique identifier. But the controlled July 31 event gives the endpoint contextual significance.

5. Independent Journalist Confirmation

On September 9, 2026, Detroit Free Press reporter Violet Ikonomova independently contacted the investigator and asked:

"did you ever figure out who Samantha Aljouny is?"

Ikonomova reported:

  • She received an email that day from the Aljouny Proton account
  • A troll image had been emailed to Conrad Mallett (then head of Detroit's Law Department)
  • Ikonomova was blind copied on that email
  • The communication came from the Aljouny Proton identity

Most critically, Ikonomova independently stated:

"makes me think it's probably phil bc its a legal thing, no idea what kevin lindke's interest would be"

She was not told to suspect anyone. Her assessment was based on the legal subject matter of the communication.

6. October 6, 2026 — The Court Filing Match

On October 6, 2026, the attorney filed a court document containing a printout of a Clutch Justice article. His own exhibit shows the article was accessed at approximately 11:54 AM.

Site records show access to the same article through Fastly/Apple Private Relay using:

FieldControlled Aljouny (Jul 31)Oct 6 Court Filing
DeviceiPhoneiPhone
OSiOS 18.7iOS 18.7
WebKit605.1.15605.1.15
Mobile ID15E14815E148
BrowserSafari 26.5Safari 26.6.1
NetworkFastlyFastly

The Safari version update (26.5 → 26.6.1) over this period is ordinary. The rest of the environment is identical.

7. What Was Sworn Under Oath

The attorney submitted a sworn affidavit stating:

  • He had never used Proton Mail
  • He had never opened a Proton account
  • He had never had a third party create or operate one for him
  • He had "no connection whatsoever" to SAljounyMediaConsulting@proton.me
  • He had never created or directed the creation of an alias, pseudonym, or "cut-out" identity

These were sworn factual representations made in litigation.

What Is Proven vs. What Is Not

Documented

  • The Aljouny ProtonMail account exists/existed
  • Its PGP key was created September 20, 2023 at 11:26:35 UTC
  • That date falls within a four-day window of Ellison's Ahmad v. UM activity
  • The attorney listed Aljouny as a potential witness
  • The attorney demanded opposing counsel admit creating the identity
  • The attorney swore he had "no connection whatsoever" to the account
  • A controlled link sent only to Aljouny was opened from an iPhone/iOS/Fastly environment
  • The same endpoint visited the site before the controlled test
  • A Detroit Free Press reporter independently received Aljouny communications
  • The reporter independently suspected the attorney based on subject matter
  • The attorney's own Oct 6 court filing matches the same technical environment
  • An IC3 complaint was filed October 6, 2026 (ID: 10f80c476ef144d4a772d0b198c75a2a)

Not Yet Proven

  • Who registered the Proton account
  • Who controlled it on each date
  • Whether the attorney personally typed every Aljouny email
  • Whether someone else had access
  • Whether the Fastly/Private Relay sessions represent one physical device

Those questions require provider/account/device evidence.

The Central Question

If provider or device evidence ultimately establishes that the attorney created, controlled, participated in, or had access to the Aljouny account, the issue becomes:

Why was a journalist being accused in court of operating an identity connected to the person making the accusation?

Sources

Every claim is sourced to:

  • Court records — Saginaw County Circuit Court, before Judge Andre Borrello
  • ProtonMail — public PGP key metadata (OpenPGP standard)
  • Bitly — controlled link access records
  • Server logs — Clutch Justice site access records
